answer.summary: productcatalogservice is the root cause, with approximately 200 ms of injected network delay. Multiple independent callers show the same step increase while server-side execution remains near-zero and successful, ruling out downstream processing stress or packet loss.

evidence: At minute 12, checkoutservice PlaceOrder jumped from a 69–95 ms baseline to 1.53 s average, later peaking at 26.665 s; checkout latency p90 reached 26.5 s while CPU remained ~0.3–0.4.

The fault affects checkoutservice calls to many independent downstreams: after onset client averages rose to 128.6 ms for Currency, 96.0 ms for Email, 161.7 ms for ProductCatalog, and 796.8 ms for Payment, while corresponding server execution remained only 0.0–0.9 ms.
Trace 6a71b31f48b69c6d9de1e0699d634c05 shows checkout waiting 26.408 s on PaymentService/Charge even though the payment server executed in 1.2 ms; the request took 26.351 s to reach payment.
Checkout socket count rose secondarily from 9 to 19 as requests remained outstanding, but there was no CPU saturation and paymentservice itself stayed fast.
answer.summary: The root cause is packet loss on checkoutservice's network path. Broad, highly variable retransmission-like delays appear across checkout's downstream RPCs while the destination services execute normally; the accumulated sockets are a consequence of those stalled calls, not socket exhaustion.

evidence: After 1705717108000, productcatalog client spans became extremely slow from every caller: frontend GetProduct max 17668 ms, frontend ListProducts max 17837 ms, recommendation ListProducts max 13804 ms.

The matching productcatalogservice server spans remained healthy (GetProduct avg 0.02 ms/max 7.31 ms; ListProducts avg 0.02 ms/max 2.51 ms), localizing the delay between callers and this service rather than in its processing.
Calls began failing with gRPC status_code 14 (Unavailable): 87 frontend GetProduct errors, 12 frontend ListProducts errors, plus recommendation/checkout errors.
Productcatalog logged "traces export: context deadline exceeded" at 1705717391000 and 1705717505000, showing its outbound network traffic was also disrupted.
CPU fell after onset (3.78 to 1.79 average), while socket count stayed at 4 until much later, ruling against CPU stress or socket exhaustion as the initiating fault.
answer.summary: The root cause is packet loss on productcatalogservice. Variable multi-second stalls, clustered completions, and gRPC Unavailable errors affected all of its callers while the service's own handlers stayed effectively instantaneous, which is characteristic of loss/retransmission rather than application delay.

The same onset raises emailservice latency-90 from ~0.005 s to ~1.626 s and its CPU from ~0.307 to ~18.734, while checkoutservice's EmailService/SendOrderConfirmation client spans rise from 4.3 ms average pre-fault to 474.3 ms post-fault.
Trace aac755338fc9649ff213982e747bf14b shows EmailService/SendOrderConfirmation taking 3397.8 ms and dominating the 3607.7 ms CheckoutService/PlaceOrder span.
answer.summary: The injected fault is memory stress in emailservice. Its working set abruptly climbs to and repeatedly hits the exact 256 MiB limit, directly slowing email handling and causing downstream checkout latency; the CPU increase is consistent with the memory stressor's allocation/churn rather than the primary fault.

evidence: At 1708489141xxx, checkoutservice p90 latency jumped from ~0.20–0.22 s to multi-second values, reaching 26.5 s, while CPU stayed ~0.3–0.4%.

Every checkout outbound dependency slowed after onset: PaymentService/Charge 7.5 ms -> 796.8 ms average (max 26.4 s), ProductCatalog GetProduct 2.4 ms -> 161.7 ms, Email 4.3 ms -> 96.0 ms, and Shipping/GetQuote 3.0 ms -> 150.2 ms.

Trace 6a71b31f48b69c6d9de1e0699d634c05 shows checkout's PaymentService/Charge client span taking 26408 ms while paymentservice itself executes it in 1.189 ms; trace 6b9963938896b04be46af6ed1d24f244 similarly shows 23740 ms client time versus 0.163 ms server time.

Checkout sockets rose from 9 to 19 as slow network calls accumulated; downstream service execution metrics remained fast. Highly variable, retransmission-scale delays rather than a fixed added latency are characteristic of packet loss.
answer.summary: Packet loss was injected into checkoutservice's network path. It caused broad, highly variable delays on all of checkout's outbound RPCs while the destination services remained healthy and fast; frontend latency/errors and socket buildup are downstream symptoms.

evidence: After ~00:01:30, currency RPC client latency degrades sharply while other downstreams remain fast: frontend CurrencyService/Convert max 26,706.4 ms and GetSupportedCurrencies max 26,647.0 ms; checkout CurrencyService/Convert max 3,599.6 ms.

Trace 9d3441535ab9cd3f61fc5e718ac60cea has a frontend CurrencyService/Convert span of 26,706.4 ms, but the matching currencyservice server span is only 0.2 ms, localizing delay to transport rather than service computation.

Long currency RPCs cluster near TCP retransmission-backoff-like durations: ~6.4 s (trace f7609d97d0351f2bbf4c5795c69f3a3c), ~13.27 s (trace 07e18e698698820a5425b62dca87be90), and ~26.71 s (trace 9d3441535ab9cd3f61fc5e718ac60cea).
Currency client calls also return gRPC status_code 14 (UNAVAILABLE) around 00:04:31 and 00:13:10, consistent with disrupted connectivity.
answer.summary: The root cause is packet loss affecting currencyservice. Calls from both frontend and checkout to currencyservice show large, retransmission-shaped network delays and occasional UNAVAILABLE responses, while currencyservice's own server handlers complete in sub-millisecond time.

At the same onset, recommendationservice memory jumps from 44,457,984 to 471,760,896 bytes, consistent with heavy buffered/page-cache I/O, and CPU later rises from about 2.47 to 19.17.
recommendationservice latency-90 rises from about 9.6 ms to about 175 ms.
Trace span /hipstershop.RecommendationService/ListRecommendations increases from 4.95 ms average before onset to 26.03 ms after; frontend client spans to it rise from 9.87 ms to 49.59 ms.
answer.summary: The injected fault is disk I/O stress in recommendationservice. Its uniquely massive disk activity begins abruptly and coincides with page-cache growth, CPU pressure, and increased recommendation RPC latency.

answer.summary: The injected fault is CPU stress in emailservice. Its CPU usage abruptly becomes saturated while request volume and non-CPU resource indicators remain stable, and its own RPC latency degrades immediately afterward.

answer.summary: The injected fault was CPU stress on recommendationservice. Its isolated, large CPU surge with unchanged request load caused local scheduling delays and downstream frontend latency, while the called product catalog service remained fast.

evidence: At 1705491665000, productcatalogservice_mem jumped abruptly from 10.3 MiB to exactly 128.0 MiB and remained highly elevated; its post-fault average was 117.9 MB versus 10.8 MB pre-fault (~11x).
The same service's CPU rose from a 3.75 pre-fault average to 18.80 post-fault (~5x), consistent with an active memory-stress workload rather than ordinary application growth.

Product-catalog client latency rose sharply after the transition: frontend GetProduct averaged 160.63 ms post-fault versus 2.57 ms pre-fault; recommendationservice ListProducts averaged 241.47 ms versus 3.46 ms.
Downstream symptoms aligned with catalog degradation: frontend p90 rose from roughly 0.17–0.21 s before the fault to roughly 2.3–3.0 s afterward.
answer.summary: The injected fault is memory stress in productcatalogservice. Its memory footprint makes a step change to 128 MiB at the incident onset, uniquely among services, followed by CPU contention and large catalog RPC latency propagated to recommendation, checkout, and frontend.

evidence: currencyservice_cpu is the only CPU series with a sustained increase: 32.235 average before the incident versus 47.994 afterward; other services' CPU stayed flat or decreased.
At essentially unchanged currencyservice workload (79.093 before vs 77.438 after), CPU ramps from ~32.8 at 1705697241000 to ~49.7 by 1705697288000 and remains near that level.
currencyservice latency degrades concurrently: p50 0.004s -> 0.059s and p90 0.052s -> 0.114s; frontend CurrencyService/Convert spans rise from 14.37ms to 70.33ms.
Downstream impact is consistent with currencyservice saturation: frontend p90 rises 0.207s -> 0.621s and checkoutservice p90 0.228s -> 0.624s.
answer.summary: The root cause is sustained CPU stress in currencyservice. Its CPU rises uniquely and persistently despite stable request load, while currency RPC and dependent frontend/checkout latencies increase at the same time.

answer.summary: The injected fault is network delay on productcatalogservice. Its callers spend tens to hundreds of milliseconds waiting while the product-catalog server handlers execute almost instantly, and the resulting latency propagates into recommendation, checkout, and frontend.

evidence: After ~1708489141000, checkoutservice outbound RPCs to every dependency became highly variable: PaymentService avg 796.8 ms/max 26408.2 ms, ProductCatalog max 3408.6 ms, Cart max 4489.2 ms, Shipping max 3152.0 ms, and Email max 1647.8 ms.

Trace 6a71b31f48b69c6d9de1e0699d634c05: checkout's PaymentService client span lasted 26408.2 ms, but the payment server span began only at the end and executed in 1.2 ms—delay occurred in checkout's network path, not payment processing.

checkoutservice PlaceOrder rose from 92.4 ms pre-fault to 2259.4 ms post-fault (max 26664.8 ms); irregular multi-second retransmission-like stalls across all checkout egress destinations are characteristic of packet loss rather than fixed latency.
checkoutservice socket count stayed at 9 through fault onset and only rose as requests accumulated, arguing against socket exhaustion as the injected cause.
answer.summary: The root cause is packet loss on checkoutservice's network path. Its outbound calls to all downstream services stall variably for up to tens of seconds while the destination server spans remain fast, producing the observed checkout and frontend latency.

The memory jump preceded secondary CPU saturation: checkoutservice_cpu rose from ~0.4 to 20.797, while latency-90 increased from ~0.2 s to 2.261 s.

After the jump, checkoutservice PlaceOrder averaged 386.7 ms versus 102.1 ms before; its calls to many otherwise healthy dependencies all slowed, and trace b50bd138553c83cd4cfdb108ab3dc5 shows PlaceOrder at 2310.9 ms.
Only frontend logged request errors (three at 1705626295000), consistent with an upstream symptom of checkout degradation rather than the root cause.
answer.summary: The injected fault was memory stress in checkoutservice. Its resident memory abruptly filled to roughly 256 MiB before CPU and checkout latency surged; broad slowdown of checkout-originated calls and frontend errors are downstream effects.
